episode_title: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom!

stories.topic: Inoculation: The Gruesome Ancestor of Vaccines
stories.summary: Smallpox killed about 25% of the children who caught it, and nearly everyone met it within the first ten or twenty years of life. People worked out that mild exposure protects. The method was to break a pustule on an infected person, cut a small wound in a healthy child's skin, and smear the white pus into it. About 10% of inoculated kids still caught smallpox and died, but 10% is less than 25%. Ajay says there is fair evidence the practice was invented in India, though it may have come from the Ottoman Empire. It likely travelled from India to the Ottomans and then to imperial courts in Europe.
stories.insight: People understood the principle of immunity long before they understood the biology. Without a way to control the dose, though, the protection came at a terrible price. Smallpox is so virulent that using a tenth or a hundredth as much pus barely changed the risk.
stories.quote: Does that sound suitably disgusting and gross and scary as hell?

stories.topic: Edward Jenner and the Cowpox Breakthrough
stories.summary: Edward Jenner noticed that women who worked with cows often caught cowpox, a mild relative of smallpox. Once they had it, they were completely protected against smallpox. Cowpox is close enough to smallpox to train the immune system but different enough not to kill. That gap is the idea behind modern vaccines, which use weakened (attenuated) pathogens, engineered carriers or synthetic molecules.
stories.insight: The real leap was not knowing that exposure protects, since inoculators already knew that. It was finding a way to get the protection without killing a large share of the people treated.
stories.quote: That was a huge intellectual breakthrough by Edward Jenner. Where the idea came that you know what this stuff can deliver protection without killing a large fraction of the people.

stories.topic: A Vaccine Designed by Software in a Day
stories.summary: Amit recalls that when COVID broke out, experts warned we might never find a vaccine. Vaccines traditionally took years or decades, and the search for an HIV vaccine is still going on. Instead, researchers in China sequenced SARS-CoV-2 and uploaded the file. A piece of software read it and printed out the design of an mRNA vaccine practically the same day. Ajay says all the remaining delay came from US FDA testing and building factories to scale up production.
stories.insight: Vaccine design has become partly an information problem. During COVID the bottlenecks were regulation and manufacturing, not the science.
stories.quote: Just pause to think of the madness of what was said, that some folks in China sequenced the SARS-CoV-2 and uploaded a file. Then a piece of software read that file and printed out the design of the mRNA vaccine.

stories.topic: Larry Brilliant, Neem Karoli Baba and India's Smallpox Fight
stories.summary: In the early 1970s, smallpox had been wiped out almost everywhere except India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Somalia. Those holdouts were a reservoir that could reinfect the world. Larry Brilliant was an American hippie living near Rishikesh with the spiritual guide Neem Karoli Baba. One day the Baba said a goddess had told him in a dream that Larry must go down to the plains and fight smallpox, and he ordered him out. Larry took an overnight bus to Delhi and reached the WHO compound at 4 a.m., with nobody there but barking dogs. He had nowhere else to go, so he slept at the gate. In the morning the staff found he had a medical degree and signed him on as a junior flunky in the smallpox programme. He eventually became one of the top people leading India's smallpox eradication programme.
stories.insight: One of the great achievements of public health in India turned partly on chance: a guru's dream and a penniless hippie sleeping at a gate. Small, odd events can have huge consequences.
stories.quote: So there is a goddess in a dream that can actually have some vast consequences for the world.

stories.topic: How the Show Got Its Name
stories.summary: The two finalists for the show's name were 'Watching the Wheels' and 'Everything is Everything'. 'Watching the Wheels' is John Lennon's song: contemplative and humble, about a universe bigger than us that trundles along while we watch with amusement. Everyone would recognise it. 'Everything is Everything' comes from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing', on The Rising, the album he wrote after the 9/11 attacks. The song matters deeply to both hosts. They tested both names on many people and chose 'Everything is Everything', judging that it could stand on its own even though most people don't know the song. Their young friend Ishaan Chintamani later sang 'Watching the Wheels' for them, and his version opens the episode.
stories.insight: In the song, the phrase points at everything the world offers while noting that the one person who matters is absent. That gives the show's title a bittersweet undertone.
stories.quote: So it's like my world is here, everything is there, but you are missing. So it is a sense of waving your hand across all the wonders of the world, Gloria Mundi.

stories.topic: Smallpox Town: A Novel That Never Got Written
stories.summary: In his early twenties, Amit read a great book on smallpox (he has forgotten the title) and a detailed New Yorker essay on the disease. That gave him an idea for a novel called 'Smallpox Town', written as one word. In it, the city itself catches smallpox, not its people. Buildings break out in pustules, the ground scabs over, and the whole course of the disease plays out on the city. He forgot the idea until Ajay's smallpox story brought it back.
stories.insight: Reading non-fiction about a disease can spark surreal fiction, and old ideas can resurface years later when a conversation touches the right nerve.
stories.quote: And in that a city get smallpox. Not the people in the city. The city gets smallpox.

recommendations.creator: Matthew Walker
recommendations.context: Amit's only recommendation of the episode. It came up after the hosts joked about the government policing people's sleep.
recommendations.reason: From it he learned that sleep-deprived drivers cause more accidents than drunk drivers. Drunk driving is dangerous, but driving while sleep deprived is even more so.

recommendations.creator: Nancy Kress
recommendations.context: Ajay's first recommendation, following the sleep discussion. He misremembers the title on air; the show notes link the Sleepless series and Beggars in Spain.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a phenomenal science fiction book. Its premise is a world with two kinds of humans: those who need to sleep and those who don't.

recommendations.item: A History of Global Health: Interventions into the Lives of Other Peoples
recommendations.creator: Randall M. Packard
recommendations.context: Ajay's second recommendation, which he calls one of the fundamental books on health.
recommendations.reason: It is one of the great books in public health, a field Ajay says is practically absent in India. India has healthcare, plus doctors trying to make health policy without having read this book. Amit adds that public health and healthcare are completely different things.

recommendations.item: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier conversation on vaccines, recorded during COVID in the fog of war.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it goes beyond vaccines and works as a potted masterclass on healthcare. It also explains the difference between public health and healthcare. He calls it 'self-recommending'.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: One of the two previous episodes that built the public-policy toolkit this episode applies to vaccines.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls this episode 'the toolkit in action'. The framework from the two earlier episodes is meant to be applied to question after question across public policy.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The companion toolkit episode: start from freedom as the default, find the market failure, then ask whether the state should intervene.
recommendations.reason: This vaccines episode is a demonstration of that method, so the earlier episode supplies the method.

recommendations.creator: John Lennon
recommendations.context: One of the two finalist names for the show. Ishaan Chintamani's cover opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: Ajay describes its mood as contemplative and humble: the universe trundles along while we watch it, curious and amused.

recommendations.creator: Chris Cornell
recommendations.context: Ishaan's first take had a grungy angst, and Amit asked Gaurav Chintamani whether Ishaan was copying Cornell.
recommendations.reason: Amit says Chris Cornell's is his favourite version of the song.

recommendations.creator: Bruce Springsteen
recommendations.context: From The Rising, the album Springsteen wrote after 9/11, and the source of the show's name.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says the song is immensely interesting and important to both hosts. Its line 'everything is everything' points at all the world's wonders while marking someone's absence.

recommendations.item: CDC Adult Immunization Schedule (vaccine list and schedule by age)
recommendations.creator: US CDC
recommendations.context: The two URLs Ajay promised in the show notes. One lists 18 adult vaccines; the other shows which to take at which age and how often boosters are needed.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls adult vaccination 'just a free lunch': prevention is better than cure. Ajay thinks the FDA is too conservative and slow, so its approval is a high bar, and its testing is a global public good. Countries like India and Bangladesh should import these vaccines.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2019 piece, linked in the show notes. In the episode he argues that vaccine price controls do more harm than good.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the argument Amit makes on air. Price controls discourage producers and innovators, always lead to scarcity, and hurt the poor more than they help.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's 2021 piece, linked in the show notes as background to the price-control discussion.
recommendations.reason: It applies the episode's argument against well-meant coercion directly to vaccine pricing during COVID.

recommendations.item: An important change of course by policy in Indian Covid-19 vaccination
recommendations.creator: Amrita Agarwal and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2021 blog piece linked in the show notes. It accompanies the discussion of letting private players supply vaccines alongside the government.
recommendations.reason: Background reading on the Indian COVID vaccine policy debate, which the hosts used as a real-world case of their argument.

recommendations.item: How the vaccine story will play out
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's 2020 piece, linked in the show notes alongside the vaccine discussion.
recommendations.reason: Further reading from Ajay on the economics of COVID vaccines, written while the pandemic was unfolding.

recommendations.creator: Albert Camus
recommendations.context: Came up while Amit was discussing his Smallpox Town idea; he quotes its famous opening line from memory.
recommendations.reason: A Camus novel Amit has read and remembers well enough to quote.

recommendations.creator: Albert Camus
recommendations.context: Came up next to Amit's Smallpox Town idea; Amit admits he hasn't read it. It is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Camus's novel of an epidemic, offered as a natural companion to a conversation about disease and imagination.

core_ideas.concept: A Vaccine Is First a Private Good
core_ideas.explanation: When you get vaccinated, you are the main beneficiary. It is like eating a chocolate or getting a toothache fixed, not something distant like clean air or foreign affairs. Self-interest alone gives people every reason to pay for vaccines. So the analysis should start from freedom and assume no state at all, then ask what, if anything, actually fails.
core_ideas.quote: A vaccine is first and foremost a private good.

core_ideas.concept: Positive Externality and the Voucher Response
core_ideas.explanation: Your vaccination also protects the people around you, which is a positive externality and therefore a market failure. The failure only matters for people who decline to pay for a vaccine. For everyone who buys one out of self-interest, there is no problem to solve. The standard fix is a voucher: the government tops up a person's own willingness to pay to reflect the benefit to everyone else. For a disease frightening enough, even that may be unnecessary, while for something like flu there are shades of grey. A positive externality justifies funding help. It does not justify state production, import bans, central planning or coercion.
core_ideas.quote: So if there is anybody in this country that sees their own self-interest and goes to a shop and gets a vaccine and gets vaccinated, we're done. Then there is no issue of market failure.

core_ideas.explanation: Education is a 'how much' decision. Because some benefits spill over to others, every single person underinvests in it, so the market failure is universal. A vaccine is a yes-or-no decision. Anyone who takes it has no market failure; the problem exists only for those who say no. That makes vaccines a much narrower case for state action than education.
core_ideas.quote: Vaccines are only integer valued. They're the zero or they're one. For the ones, it's game over.

core_ideas.concept: Only Eradication Is a Public Good
core_ideas.explanation: Most diseases can never be eradicated. The common cold moves in and out of many species, including pigs, and rabies survives in dogs and foxes. A few pathogens, such as smallpox and polio, live only in humans, so they can be wiped out. A world without smallpox meets the test of a public good. It is non-rival: one person's enjoyment doesn't reduce anyone else's. It is non-excludable: no newborn can be shut out of it. Routine vaccination only creates an externality. Eradication clears the higher bar of a public good.
core_ideas.quote: Eradication projects and only eradication projects have the high bar of public goods.

core_ideas.concept: Touching the Body Is Among the Highest Forms of State Intrusion
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay places a state touching your body on the same scale as the death penalty, torture and incarceration. That raises a moral puzzle: what if a few thousand people refuse a smallpox vaccine for religious or personal reasons? Ajay would accept significant coercion only for genuine eradication projects like smallpox and polio. Even then he calls it debatable and stresses that each person must make up their own mind.
core_ideas.quote: And a state that touches your body is a very high form of intrusive intervention.

core_ideas.concept: Judge Coercion by Principle, Not by Whether You Like the Cause
core_ideas.explanation: Amit is strongly pro-vaccine and strongly pro-freedom. He argues that the coercion he cheers today could tomorrow be used for something he opposes, so the question must be whether the forcing itself is justified, and the bar should be very high. Ajay adds that future biotechnology could give governments vaccines that make people more docile and controllable. Amit calls coercion a more widespread disease than any other.
core_ideas.quote: So we should go to the principle itself. Is the forcing good? Is the forcing bad?

core_ideas.explanation: Capping vaccine prices to help the poor discourages producers and innovators and always creates scarcity. The poor end up worse off, because a cheap vaccine you cannot find does you no good. This is coercion with good intentions and bad outcomes.
core_ideas.quote: And price controls always lead to scarcities. All it means is you won't get the damn thing.

core_ideas.concept: Let Private Supply Run Alongside the State
core_ideas.explanation: Restricting supply to the government in the name of protecting people only slows vaccination. The government can run its own programme, but private players should operate too. When richer people pay full price for privately supplied vaccines, more of the scarce cheap supply is left for people who can't afford it. Mechanisms can even be built so they subsidise others. Shutting out prices, information and incentives is what does the damage.
core_ideas.quote: If people like you and me go out there and pay a bomb for a random mRNA vaccine, in a sense, we are clearing the space for the scarce supply of the other vaccines to actually reach people who can't afford them.

core_ideas.concept: Three Ways to Build a Vaccine
core_ideas.explanation: 1. Attenuated vaccines take the pathogen and weaken it with heat, acid or other techniques, leaving just enough for the immune system to learn from. 2. Engineered carriers are the second route. The AstraZeneca vaccine, sold in India as Covishield, puts the SARS-CoV-2 spike into a chimpanzee virus that is harmless to humans and injects about a trillion particles. The body learns the spike's protein surface, so it is ready when the real virus arrives. 3. Synthetic vaccines build a new molecule that looks like the virus, and mRNA vaccines belong to this frontier. Manufactured vaccines like these carry essentially no risk of infection, whereas some attenuated vaccines sicken about one person in ten thousand.
core_ideas.quote: The idea that the human race can identify these germs, the bacteria, the viruses can construct vaccines and the vaccines can have extremely high levels of efficacy while often having near zero side effects.

core_ideas.explanation: Vaccines are not just for children, and they are not something only the government does. Treat them like sleep hygiene, nutrition and exercise. A whole range of adult vaccines exists. Talk about them, post them on Instagram and give others FOMO. Their friend Rajeshwari Sengupta paid for 42 vaccines for her child. Paying upfront to rule out diseases is, in Ajay's words, a free lunch.
core_ideas.quote: Vaccines are not a zone of government. They should be a zone of the people.

core_ideas.concept: FDA Approval as a Global Public Good
core_ideas.explanation: The US FDA does the expensive testing and publishes the results, so every country can benefit for free. Ajay thinks the FDA is too conservative and slow, which makes its approval a high bar. Countries like India and Bangladesh should simply import approved vaccines from global manufacturers instead of chasing self-reliance.
core_ideas.quote: So something being approved by the US FDA is a high bar. And this is a global public good because they've done the hard work of the testing.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the bureaucratic mind: 'there's nothing as attractive to a bureaucrat as the thought of a government program.' Whisper 'government program, committee, budget' in their ear before bed, and 'they'll go to sleep with a beatific smile on their face and their wife will think they're having an affair.'

Amit on Ajay's mumbling: Ajay once told him to take 'the influencer vaccine'. Amit replied: 'There's a vaccine that protects me from influencers. I'm signing up, give it to me. You had me at hello.' Ajay had actually said influenza.
After listing the popular myths about state-run vaccination, Amit says: 'My blood is already boiling. It's a good time to inject me with pus.'

Ajay pictures state officials 'strapping down Amit Bhai' as he hollers and screams, 'a scene straight out of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.' Amit: 'which Amit Bhai are you talking about? It better not be me.' Later Amit adds: 'You really want to strap me down, don't you?'
On Larry Brilliant landing a job at the WHO: 'He was brilliant. He was very brilliant. He was not just brilliant, he was very brilliant.'
Amit's alternative explanation for the guru's dream: perhaps Larry Brilliant hadn't bathed in three days and Neem Karoli Baba simply made up the goddess to get rid of him. Ajay: 'Enough is enough.'

Amit clarifies that 'adult vaccines' doesn't mean 'vaccines that have grown up.' Ajay: 'Or a vaccine that makes sure that you'll never be an adult.' Amit: 'That would be an excellent vaccine as well.'

The sleep nanny state. Amit imagines the government scolding him: 'Ajay Shah you slept seven hours, thirty five minutes... You need to get your two hours of REM.' Ajay goes further: sleepy drivers impose a negative externality, so your phone tells your sleep tracker, which tells your car not to start. Amit: 'What have you done, Ajay Shah, this is the beginning of the end.'
'You are never too old to have a happy childhood.' Amit credits the line to Ajay, who admits it's 'stolen'. Ajay's joke that follows is a vaccine that makes sure you'll never be an adult.
Ajay explains the intuition behind inoculation with 'as the old Greek saying goes, that which does not destroy you makes you stronger.'
Albert Camus's L'Etranger: Amit recites its opening, 'my mother died today, or was it yesterday', while admitting he hasn't read The Plague.

Ishaan Chintamani, son of Gaurav Chintamani, covers Lennon's 'Watching the Wheels' at the top of the episode, and two more takes play at the end. Amit thought Ishaan's grungy chorus was borrowed from Chris Cornell's version, his favourite. Gaurav explained that Ishaan had heard both Lennon and Cornell and made the song his own.
Tyler Cowen's 'self-recommending': Amit borrows it to plug his own Seen and the Unseen episode, adding, 'but I don't think he means this.'
